section.title: The Foolish Shepherd
section.sectionRationale: The dark heart of the first burden. Zechariah acts out the role of a good shepherd of a doomed flock, is rejected, and is paid off with thirty pieces of silver, thrown to the potter in the house of the LORD. Matthew sees this fulfilled in Judas's betrayal price for Christ. When the good Shepherd is spurned, a worthless shepherd is raised up instead.
section.thesis: When God's people reject the good Shepherd and value Him at the contemptible price of a slave, they forfeit favor and union and are handed over to a worthless shepherd, a rejection fulfilled when Christ was betrayed for thirty pieces of silver.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the wailing over the doomed land; the shepherd of the flock marked for slaughter, his two staffs Favor and Union broken, and the thirty pieces of silver thrown to the potter; and the raising up of the worthless shepherd, ending in woe upon him.

verses.text: Open your doors, O Lebanon, that the fire may consume your cedars!
Wail, O cypress, for the cedar has fallen; the majestic trees are ruined! Wail, O oaks of Bashan, for the dense forest has been cut down!
Listen to the wailing of the shepherds, for their glory is in ruins. Listen to the roaring of the young lions, for the thickets of the Jordan are destroyed.
This is what the LORD my God says: “Pasture the flock marked for slaughter,
whose buyers slaughter them without remorse. Those who sell them say, ‘Blessed be the LORD, for I am rich!’ Even their own shepherds have no compassion on them.

For I will no longer have compassion on the people of the land, declares the LORD, but behold, I will cause each man to fall into the hands of his neighbor and his king, who will devastate the land, and I will not deliver it from their hands.”

So I pastured the flock marked for slaughter, especially the afflicted of the flock. Then I took for myself two staffs, calling one {{noam|Favor}} and the other {{chovlim|Union}}, and I pastured the flock.
And in one month I dismissed three shepherds. My soul grew impatient with the flock, and their souls also detested me.
Then I said, “I will no longer shepherd you. Let the dying die, and the perishing perish; and let those who remain devour one another's flesh.”
Next I took my staff called Favor and cut it in two, revoking the covenant I had made with all the nations.
It was revoked on that day, and so the afflicted of the flock who were watching me knew that it was the word of the LORD.
Then I told them, “If it seems right to you, give me my wages; but if not, keep them.” So they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of {{keseph|silver}}.

And the LORD said to me, “Throw it to the potter,” this magnificent price at which they valued me. So I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them to the {{yotser|potter}} in the house of the LORD.
Then I cut in two my second staff called Union, breaking the brotherhood between Judah and Israel.

units.label: The worthless shepherd
units.note: woe to the one who deserts the flock

verses.text: And the LORD said to me: “Take up once more the equipment of a foolish shepherd.

For behold, I will raise up a shepherd in the land who will neither care for the lost, nor seek the young, nor heal the broken, nor sustain the healthy, but he will devour the flesh of the choice sheep and tear off their hooves.
Woe to the worthless shepherd, who deserts the flock! May a sword strike his arm and his right eye! May his arm be completely withered and his right eye utterly blinded!”

noam.gloss: Favor, pleasantness, graciousness, delight. The first shepherd's staff is named Favor, representing God's gracious protection of His flock, including a restraining covenant over the nations. Cutting it in two dramatizes the withdrawal of that gracious protection when the good Shepherd is rejected, leaving the flock exposed to the nations.

chovlim.gloss: Bonds, ties, union. The second staff is named Union, representing the God-given brotherhood binding His people together, especially Judah and Israel. Breaking it pictures the shattering of that unity, the community torn apart, when they spurn their Shepherd. Grace withdrawn and union broken are the twin consequences of rejecting the good Shepherd.

keseph.gloss: Silver, money. Thirty pieces of silver was the compensation for a slave gored by an ox in the law of Exodus, a contemptibly low valuation. To weigh out this sum as the Shepherd's wages is to insult Him, valuing the LORD's servant at the price of a slave. Matthew sees the exact price fulfilled in the thirty silver coins paid to betray Jesus.

yotser.gloss: A potter, a maker of clay vessels. Throwing the silver to the potter in the house of the LORD signals contemptuous disposal of a shameful price, discarded to a lowly craftsman at the temple. Matthew records that the betrayal money was used to buy the potter's field, tying this action directly to the burial ground purchased with Judas's coins.

basic.context: This is the darkest chapter of the first burden. After a poem wailing over a doomed land, Zechariah is told to act out the role of a shepherd over a flock marked for slaughter, a flock exploited by its sellers and its own shepherds. He takes two staffs, Favor and Union. The flock detests him, so he resigns, breaks the staff Favor, and asks for his wages. They weigh out thirty pieces of silver, the price of a slave, an insult. God tells him to throw it to the potter in the temple. He breaks Union too. Then God raises up a worthless shepherd instead, and pronounces woe on him.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a prophetic sign-act, acted out and heavy with symbolism. The good shepherd represents God's true care rejected by the people. The two staffs picture God's gracious protection and the people's unity, both broken by their rejection. The thirty pieces of silver and the potter are read by Matthew as fulfilled in the betrayal of Jesus. The worthless shepherd raised up in place of the good one warns of judgment through bad leadership.
basic.originalLanguages: The two staffs are named noam, Favor, God's gracious protection, and chovlim, Union, the bond of brotherhood, both cut in two. The Shepherd's wage is thirty pieces of keseph, silver, the compensation for a slave, a contemptuous price. And it is thrown to the yotser, the potter, in the temple, an image of shameful disposal Matthew ties to the potter's field.
basic.typology: The good shepherd rejected and valued at a slave's price is fulfilled in Jesus, betrayed for thirty pieces of silver. The money thrown to the potter is fulfilled in the potter's field bought with the betrayal money. The worthless shepherd raised up when the good one is spurned points toward the ultimate false shepherd, the antichrist, who devours rather than feeds.
basic.christ: Matthew explicitly connects this chapter to Christ. The thirty pieces of silver weighed out as the Shepherd's insulting wage is the exact sum Judas received to betray Jesus, and the coins, thrown down in the temple, were used to buy the potter's field. The good Shepherd, priced at the value of a slave and rejected by His own, is the Lord Jesus. When He is spurned, grace and union are broken, and a devouring shepherd takes His place.
basic.god: God feels the insult of rejected shepherd-love, and He is just in the consequences: when His care is despised, His gracious protection and the people's unity are withdrawn, and they are handed over to leaders who exploit them. Yet even the price of His Shepherd's rejection becomes part of His sovereign plan, foretold in exact detail and fulfilled in Christ.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 27 records the thirty pieces of silver and the potter's field, citing this prophecy. Matthew 26 tells of Judas's betrayal price. John 1 says He came to His own and His own did not receive Him. John 10 contrasts the good Shepherd with the hireling who abandons the sheep.
basic.oneStory: The good Shepherd is rejected and valued at a slave's price, and grace and union are broken, so a worthless shepherd is raised up. This is fulfilled when Christ is betrayed for thirty pieces of silver, spurned by His own. The story bends toward the cross, where the rejected Shepherd lays down His life, and warns of the false shepherd who must finally be judged.

context.literary:
Chapter 11 is the shortest road from hope to tragedy in the whole book. It begins with a poem in verses 1 to 3, a three-line dirge that opens with a command to a mountain, 'Open your doors, O Lebanon,' and goes on to forests wailing, shepherds howling and lions roaring. Then comes a sign-act in verses 4 to 14, narrated in the first person, and a second sign-act in verses 15 to 17, where the prophet is told to take up a different set of tools. The chapter therefore has a poem, a long prose-like narration and a shorter closing oracle, and each part is a different angle on the same event.

The poem in verses 1 to 3 works as a kind of overture. The cedars of Lebanon and the oaks of Bashan are the tallest and strongest trees known to the Israelite ear, and in other prophets they stand for human pride, Isaiah 2:12 and 13. The lions' thicket in the Jordan valley adds another image of what is lush and dangerous. When these fall, the 'shepherds' who howl in verse 3 are the leaders whose pasture has been burned. The poem does not say who is burning the land, and it leaves the sense of ruin hanging.

The sign-act that follows is the heart of the chapter. The first lines, 4 to 6, give God's commission and the reason for it: a flock sold and slaughtered by people who bless God for the profit. Verses 7 to 14 then narrate the prophet's obedience step by step, the pasturing, the staffs, the dismissal of three shepherds, the resignation, the payment, the throwing of the money, the second breaking. It is a story told in a flat, factual voice, and the flatness makes the events heavier.

The structure of the two staffs is symmetrical. Favor is taken in verse 7 and broken in verse 10, with its meaning explained in verse 10, and Union is taken in the same verse and broken in verse 14. Between the two breakings sit the wages and the potter, the moment of price, so that the betrayal is set in the centre of the structure.

The last movement, verses 15 to 17, begins with a command to take 'once more' the equipment of a foolish shepherd. The word 'once more' links to the earlier sign and shows that the prophet will now play the opposite part. Where the good shepherd was rejected, the bad one is permitted. The chapter ends with a woe, and that woe stops the narrative.
context.historical:
The first poem draws on the geography of the north and east of the land: Lebanon, with its cedars, Bashan, east of Galilee, with its oaks, and the thickets along the Jordan where lions lived. Jeremiah 12:5 and 49:19 use the Jordan thicket as the place of danger and pride. A hearer would picture the whole northern landscape in flames and see in it the fall of the pride of the land.

The commission in verses 4 to 6 speaks of a flock 'marked for slaughter,' with buyers who feel no guilt, sellers who thank God for their wealth and shepherds without compassion. It is a picture of an economy that treats people as stock. The prophets had long said this of Israel's powerful, as in Amos 2:6, where the needy are sold for a pair of sandals. The verse 6 prediction that each man will fall into the hand of his neighbour and his king has been read in several ways. Some see the strife of the generations after the exile; others see the civil factions and foreign rulers that tore the nation apart in the first century AD, when the siege of Jerusalem brought neighbour against neighbour and, in the end, the chief priests said, 'We have no king but Caesar,' John 19:15.

The 'thirty pieces of silver' was a recognised sum. Exodus 21:32 sets thirty shekels as the compensation owed to a master when a slave is gored by an ox, so that the price put on the shepherd was the price of a slave's life. To be valued at that price was an insult dressed as payment.

The potter is a familiar figure in the prophets. Jeremiah's own visits to a potter, Jeremiah 18:1 to 6, and to buy a clay jar, Jeremiah 19:1 and 2, make the potter an established part of the prophetic vocabulary. There is also a textual question: some ancient witnesses read 'the treasury' where the Hebrew has 'the potter.' The two words differ by a single letter.
context.canonical:
The shepherd imagery connects the chapter to Ezekiel 34, which condemns the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves, and to Jeremiah 23:1 and 2, 'Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of My pasture.' Zechariah goes beyond both by having the prophet himself play the shepherd, so that the good shepherd is a figure to be seen on the stage and not only promised. The theme ends in Zechariah 13:7, 'Awake, O sword, against My Shepherd,' which Jesus quotes in Mark 14:27 on the night before His death.

The thirty pieces of silver carry the Old Testament price of a slave from Exodus 21:32 into the New Testament. Matthew 26:14 and 15 says the chief priests 'set out for him thirty pieces of silver' when Judas offered to betray Jesus, and Matthew 27:3 to 10 says that Judas threw the silver into the temple and that the priests used it to buy the potter's field. The quotation in Matthew 27:9 and 10 is introduced as spoken 'through Jeremiah the prophet,' and it draws on Zechariah 11:12 and 13 with allusions to Jeremiah's potter and his purchase of a field, Jeremiah 32:6 to 9. Acts 1:18 and 19 gives a second account of the field.

The worthless shepherd is a figure that rises again in Scripture. Jesus warns, 'if someone else comes in his own name, you will receive him,' John 5:43. John writes of the antichrist who is coming and the many antichrists already here, 1 John 2:18, and Paul of the man of lawlessness who seats himself in the temple, 2 Thessalonians 2:3 and 4. Zechariah's picture of a shepherd who devours the sheep is the model for these later portraits.

The chapter's central tragedy, a people who reject the one sent to care for them, is also in John 1:11, 'His own did not receive Him,' and in Jesus' lament over Jerusalem, Matthew 23:37 and 38 and Luke 19:41 to 44. The pattern runs from Samuel's day, when the people's demand for a king was in truth a rejection of God, 1 Samuel 8:7, to the day when they said they had no king but Caesar.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The prophet wanted Israel to feel the weight of what they had done with their shepherd. A sign-act in the Old Testament is not a mere illustration. When Ezekiel lay on his side or Jeremiah wore a yoke, the people saw the word enacted. Here Zechariah plays the role of the shepherd God sends, and in doing so shows the community its own response. The flock detests him, he is paid a slave's price, and he has to break the bonds that had kept the people safe and united. The first hearers were meant to see themselves in the flock and to be shocked.

He also wanted them to see that rejection has consequences that run through the community. When the good shepherd steps aside, the flock does not become free; it falls into the hands of neighbours, kings and a worthless shepherd. The loss of Favor means the loss of the protection that held the nations back from harming Israel, and the loss of Union means that Judah and Israel are divided. Everything the prophet has been promising in chapters 9 and 10 is put at risk by the refusal in chapter 11.

At a deeper level the author is interested in the character of God. The price paid was an insult, and God's word to the prophet is to throw it to the potter, with 'this magnificent price' said with biting irony. God is not indifferent to what His shepherd is worth, and the pain is His.

Finally, the closing woe makes the point that leaders who desert their flock will not escape. The final lines are a curse on the arm and the eye, the very parts a shepherd needs to protect and to see. The aim is to warn leaders and to console the flock: the God who watches has not forgotten either.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is a strange mix of narrative and command, and it is easy to read it wrongly. The sign-act is a prophetic drama. It is not a model for how pastors or believers should behave. Zechariah breaks staffs because God tells him to, and the New Testament never takes this as a pattern for church life. The same applies to the final command to take up the tools of a foolish shepherd, which is a prophetic role and not a recommendation for anyone to follow.

What the chapter does describe is the fate of those who despise God's gracious care. It is descriptive of a particular moment in Israel's history, and it gains its force from the New Testament's claim that it was fulfilled in Christ's betrayal. The abiding point is the seriousness of rejecting the one God sends.

The chapter also offers a test for leaders. The description of the worthless shepherd, who neither cares for the lost nor seeks the young nor heals the broken nor sustains the healthy, reads like a checklist of what a shepherd should do. Taken as description it says what is wrong with false leaders, and taken as instruction in the negative it says what Christian shepherds are for. Peter tells elders to 'be shepherds of God's flock' and not to lord it over those entrusted to them, 1 Peter 5:2 and 3, and Paul tells the Ephesian elders to keep watch, Acts 20:28.

There is also a caution against reading the horror of verse 9, 'let those who remain devour one another's flesh,' as a prediction about any one event or as an excuse for contempt. It echoes the covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28:53, and it describes the depth of the collapse and not an instruction.

debates.question: How does Matthew's quotation relate to Jeremiah and Zechariah?

views.label: A blended citation labelled with the major prophet
views.case: Matthew names Jeremiah but the words about thirty pieces of silver come from Zechariah 11:12 and 13. Jewish writers often cited a collection of prophets under the name of the best-known one, and Jeremiah's own scenes with a potter, a clay jar and a field, Jeremiah 18, 19 and 32, are woven into the picture. This reading takes Matthew to be fusing the two.

views.label: Zechariah is the controlling text
views.case: The silver and the potter are from Zechariah and the allusion to Jeremiah gives it a prophetic backing and a thematic frame, so Matthew's formula points to the prophetic scroll rather than a precise text.

views.label: A textual or scribal variation
views.case: Some ancient copyists wrote Zechariah or left out the name, and some suggest that the name Jeremiah was in Matthew's source. This view treats the difficulty as a small textual matter that does not affect the meaning.

debates.bearing: Every view agrees that Zechariah 11:12 and 13 stands behind the thirty pieces of silver and the potter's field in Matthew 27, and that the story is read as a fulfilment of prophecy.

debates.question: Who is the worthless shepherd of verses 15 to 17?

views.label: A bad human ruler or succession of rulers in Israel's history
views.case: The passage describes the rulers who fell upon the people after the good shepherd was refused: foreign kings and local tyrants who took without caring. This reading treats the shepherd as a type of oppressive leadership in general.

views.label: The final antichrist
views.case: The shepherd who deserts the flock stands over against Christ and is read alongside Jesus' words in John 5:43 and the man of lawlessness in 2 Thessalonians 2:3 and 4. Verse 17's judgment on his arm and right eye is read as his final defeat.

views.label: The rejected people's own leaders, including those who delivered Christ up
views.case: Some link the worthless shepherd with the leaders who rejected Jesus and with the later destruction of Jerusalem, in which the people fell into the hands of their neighbour and their king, as verse 6 says.

debates.bearing: Each view sees that a people who refuse God's Shepherd will be ruled by a poor one. It warns against trust in leaders who profit from the flock.

debates.question: What are the three shepherds dismissed in one month, verse 8?

views.label: Three offices, such as prophet, priest and king
views.case: The three shepherds are the three kinds of leader in Israel, removed together as the people turned from God's care. The month is a short span, suggesting swift judgment.

views.label: Three particular rulers or classes of leader in the history of the period
views.case: Interpreters have proposed various sets of three, but the text names none of them, which makes any identification a guess.

views.label: A symbolic number for complete removal of failed leadership
views.case: Three and one month are literary figures for a thorough and rapid clearing, and the point lies in the swiftness, not in a list of names.

debates.bearing: Readers have offered a great many identifications, and the text does not say. It is wiser to hold the lesson than to claim the answer.

study.originalLanguages:
The sign-act begins with a commission whose key word is ro'eh, the shepherd's verb 'pasture,' and its object, tson haharegah, 'the flock of slaughter.' The noun harega comes from the verb for killing and appears in Jeremiah 12:3 and 7:32, where it names the 'Valley of Slaughter.' The flock is not simply doomed; it is already assigned to the butcher, and the shepherd is asked to feed animals who are on their way to the block. That is an odd commission, and its oddness is the point. God sends a good shepherd to a flock that has been sold.

In verse 7 the BSB says 'the afflicted of the flock.' The Hebrew word is the same family as the 'humble' of Zechariah 9:9. The King who comes to Zion is ani, and so are the sheep he pastors. Some interpreters read the line a little differently, as 'the sheep traders' by dividing the consonants another way, which would suit the sellers of verse 5. The BSB reading gives a link with the earlier chapter: the humble King shepherds the humble flock.

Verse 8 uses two strong words for the breakdown of the relationship. 'My soul grew impatient' is a phrase built on the root qatsar, 'to be short,' so that the prophet's patience runs short. In the next clause the flock's souls 'detested' him, a word of loathing. The shepherd and flock are in mutual revulsion, and the idiom of the soul stresses that the feeling is deep.

The covenant in verse 10 is a berit, and what is revoked is a covenant 'with all the nations,' in Hebrew kol ha'ammim, 'all the peoples.' The plural 'peoples' is the word usually used of the nations around Israel, and the covenant may be a protection that God had set around His people from the powers that surrounded them. When Favor, noam, is cut, the protection is gone. The verb in verse 10 is a verb of cutting, and covenants in Hebrew are 'cut' too, so that the staff and the covenant fall under one stroke.

The wages in verse 12 are sekhar, and the sum is thirty pieces of silver, shloshim kesef. The thirty is the sum paid for a slave who has been killed by an ox, Exodus 21:32. In verse 13 God says, 'this magnificent price,' adder hayyeqar, and the sarcasm is plain. The Hebrew word for 'magnificent' is a word of glory, and it is thrown in the face of the buyers. Then the prophet 'threw' the silver, using the verb shalak, 'to cast, hurl,' not to place or to give. And it goes to the yotser, 'the potter,' though some ancient witnesses read otser, 'the treasury,' which would differ from the Hebrew by one letter and would fit Matthew 27:6, where the priests refuse to put the money into the treasury. The text of the Hebrew Bible keeps 'potter,' and the potter's field of Matthew 27:7 matches it.

The second staff, chovlim, in verse 14 is a plural noun meaning 'cords' or 'bands,' a word that in other places means 'pangs' or 'ropes,' and the BSB gives the sense 'Union.' The verb 'breaking' the 'brotherhood,' achvah, between Judah and Israel means the severing of the bond of kinship.

In verse 17 the 'worthless shepherd' is ro'i ha'elil. The word elil is the one the law uses for idols, 'worthless things,' Leviticus 19:4. A worthless shepherd is, literally, an idol of a shepherd, a nothing posing as something. This picks up the idols of 10:2, which 'speak deceit.' The leader who looks like a shepherd and is not belongs with the images that look like gods and are not. The shepherd 'deserts' the flock with the verb azav, to leave or abandon, and the woe falls on the arm and the right eye, the parts that wield the staff and watch for danger.

typology.type: The shepherd valued at thirty pieces of silver, verses 12 and 13
typology.fulfillment: The Old Testament sum for a slave killed by an ox, Exodus 21:32, is the price put on the prophet-shepherd. In the Gospels the same sum is agreed with the chief priests when Judas offers to hand Jesus over, Matthew 26:14 and 15. Matthew then connects the silver with Zechariah, Matthew 27:9 and 10. The escalation is that the One valued at a slave's price is the Lord of glory, who took 'the form of a servant,' Philippians 2:7. The type is not exact in every detail: Zechariah is paid his wages in person, while Jesus is betrayed by a disciple, and the fit lies in the price and the contempt.

typology.type: The silver thrown into the house of the LORD and given to the potter, verse 13
typology.fulfillment: The prophet throws the money into the temple, and Judas, seized with remorse, throws the silver into the temple, Matthew 27:5. The priests will not put blood money in the treasury and buy the potter's field with it as a burial place for foreigners, Matthew 27:6 and 7. The correspondence is of the temple, the throwing and the potter. The escalation is an irony: the money that priced a Messiah ends up buying a resting place for foreigners, which some readers take as a quiet sign of the welcome later given to the Gentiles, though Matthew does not say so. The type has limits, since Zechariah's potter is a short note, while Matthew's account carries the weight of a field still known by a name, the Field of Blood, Acts 1:19.

typology.type: The staff Favor broken and the covenant revoked, verses 10 and 11
typology.fulfillment: The breaking of Favor withdraws a protection, and the afflicted of the flock who watched know that it is the word of the LORD. Jesus weeps over a city that did not know the time of its visitation and says its house will be left desolate, Luke 19:41 to 44 and Matthew 23:37 and 38. The pattern of a withdrawn favour fulfils itself in the destruction that followed. The type points beyond a single judgment: in Christ the covenant is not simply withdrawn but renewed in His blood, Luke 22:20, so that the breaking of the staff finds its answer in the breaking of the body.

typology.type: The shepherd who deserts the flock, verses 16 and 17
typology.fulfillment: The worthless shepherd is the opposite of the good shepherd. Jesus contrasts Himself with the hired hand who sees the wolf, abandons the sheep and runs, John 10:12 and 13, and with those who come in their own name, John 5:43. The picture reaches its extreme in the 'man of lawlessness' of 2 Thessalonians 2:3 and 4 and the antichrists of 1 John 2:18. The correspondence is of character: self-interest dressed as care. The type is incomplete in that Zechariah gives no name or date, and the New Testament speaks of such figures as already present and still to come.

study.christ:
This is the chapter in which the Old Testament comes closest to describing the Cross before it happens, and it comes through a sign and a price. A shepherd tends a flock that is marked for slaughter. The flock detests him. He asks for his wages and is paid the price of a slave. He throws the money into the house of the LORD. The Gospel writers did not make this up from nothing; they found a prophetic text that had been waiting for such a story. The New Testament draws three links.

The first is the Shepherd himself. Chapter 11 tells us that the one sent to care for God's flock would be rejected, and the Gospels tell us the same. 'He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him,' John 1:11. Jesus said, 'I am the good shepherd,' and the good shepherd 'lays down His life for the sheep,' John 10:11. When the Pharisees and the priests heard Him, they did not want Him, and the rejection reached its climax in the cry before Pilate, 'We have no king but Caesar,' John 19:15. Jesus Himself wept over the city that would not be gathered, Matthew 23:37. The prophet's role as a shepherd who is not wanted is a pattern in which Jesus fits.

The second link is the price. Matthew's telling of Judas and the chief priests is almost a retelling of Zechariah 11:12 and 13: the wages, the thirty pieces of silver, the throwing of them in the temple and the potter's field, Matthew 26:14 and 15 and 27:3 to 10. The price is the slave's price of Exodus 21:32. The One who 'emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant,' Philippians 2:7, was valued as a servant who had been killed by a careless animal. The irony is that this cheap price is what God uses to buy a field for strangers, and the field becomes the sign of a purchase greater than the field. Peter says believers were ransomed by 'the precious blood of Christ,' 1 Peter 1:18 and 19.

The third link is the breaking of the staffs. When the shepherd gives up the staff Favor, the flock loses its protection, and when he breaks Union the bond between Judah and Israel is cut. The New Testament shows what follows from the rejection of Christ in its own history: a city left desolate, Luke 19:43 and 44, and an end to the old arrangement of temple and sacrifice. Yet in His own death Christ also makes the two one again. He breaks down the dividing wall, Ephesians 2:14, and gathers into one the children of God, John 11:52. The Shepherd is struck, as Zechariah 13:7 says, and the flock is scattered, Mark 14:27, but after He rises they are gathered again.

There is also a lesson in the contrast with the worthless shepherd. Christ is the one who cares for the lost, seeks the young, heals the broken and sustains the healthy. The tasks listed in verse 16 as undone by the false shepherd are the very tasks Jesus does in the Gospels: He seeks the lost sheep, Luke 15:4 to 6, proclaims release to the oppressed, Luke 4:18, and feeds the crowds, Mark 6:34 to 44. The negative picture is a portrait in reverse.

A reader should be careful. The passage does not name Jesus and the first hearers would have read it as a story of their own history. Nor is every detail in the chapter a coded reference to His life; the two staffs and the three shepherds are not allegories to be decoded. The connection to Christ stands on the specific points that the New Testament itself names, the price, the potter, the rejection of the shepherd, and on the larger pattern that runs through Scripture.
study.god:
The first thing this chapter shows about God is that He is a God who feels. The commission is given with a bitter phrase, 'this magnificent price at which they valued me,' and the 'me' is the LORD's. The prophet is playing the shepherd, but the insult is aimed at God. A God who can be insulted is a God who is personally involved with His people, who gave them care and is hurt by their contempt. The Bible does not shy away from this picture, and it should shape how we think of God's love. His love is real enough to be wounded.

He is a God who judges with His eyes open. The flock is not innocent; the sellers say 'Blessed be the LORD, for I am rich!' and the shepherds have no compassion. God tells the prophet, 'I will no longer have compassion on the people of the land,' verse 6. This is not the sudden withdrawal of a fickle ruler. It follows a long run of warnings and a real offer of care. The prophet pastured the flock, took two staffs, and tried. The judgment comes after the offer, and the offer was sincere.

He is a God who hands people over to what they choose. 'I will cause each man to fall into the hands of his neighbor and his king,' verse 6. The judgment is the removal of restraint. The people who rejected the Shepherd receive the consequence in the form of what they preferred, as Paul says in Romans 1:24 and 26 and 28 of those whom God 'gave over.' This is a sober doctrine, and it keeps God just without making Him cruel.

He is a God who is sovereign even over betrayal. The thirty pieces of silver are a human act of contempt, and God says, 'Throw it to the potter.' The word of God turns the insult into an instrument. The New Testament says the same of the cross: Jesus was 'delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge,' Acts 2:23, and the people who did it were responsible. God does not cause the sin but is not defeated by it. He holds together real human guilt and a purpose that is never thwarted.

He is a God who cares about leaders. The closing woe is stern. The arm that should defend the sheep is to wither and the eye that should watch for danger is to go dark. God watches those who handle His flock, and He will not let them off. This is a warning to every shepherd and an assurance to every sheep. In Ezekiel 34:8 He says that He knows what has happened to His flock because the shepherds fed themselves, and He will act.

And He is a God whose purposes do not fail with the failure of the people. The chapter is dark, but it sits between chapter 10, where God promises to gather and save, and chapter 12, where He will pour out a spirit of grace. The breaking of the staffs is not the last word. God's plans work through rejection and arrive at the hope of the later chapters.

For worship, this chapter asks us to hold a sober awe at the cost of the Shepherd. The right response to the thirty pieces of silver is not to look for a villain among others but to see ourselves as part of the flock who valued Him at so little, and to be grateful that the Shepherd gave Himself anyway.

crossReferences.note: The law sets thirty shekels of silver as the compensation for a servant killed by an ox. This is the background of the price in Zechariah 11:12: the flock values its shepherd at what a careless owner would pay for a dead slave. It explains why the price is an insult, and why God calls it 'magnificent' with bitter irony.

Jeremiah visits a potter's house and sees clay reshaped on the wheel. The potter is a figure of God's sovereign shaping of His people. It stands behind Matthew's mention of Jeremiah in connection with Zechariah 11:13, and it gives the potter in Zechariah a prophetic setting.

Jeremiah buys a field at Anathoth, weighing out silver, as a sign that the land will again be bought and sold. It is the other Jeremiah passage that gives Matthew 27:9 and 10 its wording about a field bought with silver, and it helps to explain why Matthew names Jeremiah.

The shepherds of Israel who feed themselves while the flock goes without are condemned. Zechariah 11:4 to 6 and 15 to 17 are cut from the same cloth. The Ezekiel passage lists the failures, such as not strengthening the weak or searching for the lost, which Zechariah repeats in his portrait of the worthless shepherd.

God calls the sword against 'My Shepherd,' the man who is His Companion, and says the sheep will be scattered. It carries the chapter's story forward: the Shepherd rejected in chapter 11 is struck in chapter 13. Jesus quotes it on the night of His arrest, Mark 14:27.

Judas goes to the chief priests, asks what they will give him, and is paid thirty pieces of silver. Matthew places the price at the start of the passion and uses the words of Zechariah 11:12 almost exactly. It is the first place where the prophecy of the silver begins to come true.

Judas returns the silver, throws it into the temple, and the priests buy the potter's field with it. Matthew says this fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah, drawing on Zechariah 11:12 and 13. It is the New Testament's own explanation of how the chapter points to Jesus, and it joins the two prophets in a single citation.

'He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him.' This is the summary of Zechariah 11 on the lips of the Gospel writer. The Shepherd comes to His flock and is refused, which is what the sign-act enacts. John's sentence sets the rejection at the opening of the story and not only at the end.

Jesus contrasts the good shepherd who lays down His life with the hired hand who abandons the sheep when the wolf comes. The hired hand is the New Testament form of the worthless shepherd of Zechariah 11:16 and 17, who deserts the flock. Jesus shows by contrast what a true shepherd does.

Jesus laments that He longed to gather Jerusalem's children as a hen gathers her chicks, 'but you were unwilling,' and says their house is left desolate. This is the sorrow behind Zechariah 11: the Shepherd offers care, is refused, and the consequence is the loss of the city's protection.

Jesus weeps over the city because it did not recognize the time of its visitation, and describes the siege to come. It matches the withdrawal of Favor in Zechariah 11:10 and the handing over to neighbour and king in verse 6, as the history that followed Jesus' rejection.

Paul writes of the 'man of lawlessness' who exalts himself and sits in the temple of God. This is the final, personal form of the worthless shepherd that some readers see in Zechariah 11:15 to 17. The link is the pattern, a false leader who takes the place that belongs to God.

study.oneStory:
The chapter belongs to the oldest question in the Bible: who will care for the creature made in God's image? Genesis 1 and 2 show God Himself placing the man in the garden to work it and keep it, Genesis 2:15, and the language of keeping is the language of the shepherd. After the fall the work of caring for the flock passes to human rulers, and the history of Israel's kings is a history of shepherds who either fed the flock or fed on it. Samuel warned that a king would take, 1 Samuel 8:11 to 18, and by the time of the exile the verdict was in: the shepherds had destroyed and scattered the sheep, Jeremiah 23:1.

Zechariah 11 answers this history in a way that is shocking and necessary. God sends a Shepherd of His own, and He is rejected. This is the same pattern as the prophets who were stoned, the Servant who was despised and rejected, Isaiah 53:3, and the Son sent last of all in the parable of the tenants. The Bible does not hide the cost of the rescue it is describing. The rescue passes through rejection.

The chapter sets up what follows within the book. Chapter 12 turns to the day when God pours out a spirit of grace and the people look on the One they have pierced, Zechariah 12:10, and chapter 13 describes the Shepherd struck and the sheep scattered. The tragedy of chapter 11 is therefore the dark centre of a larger turn. The staff that was broken is followed by a fountain opened for cleansing, Zechariah 13:1, and the refusal gives way to grief, and grief to grace.

In the wider story the chapter sets up the cross. The betrayal for silver, the throwing of the coins and the potter's field are the details of the last week of Jesus, and they show that even the things done against Him were within what Scripture had foreseen. The Shepherd is struck, and by that striking He lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11. The old pattern of rejection becomes the means of redemption.

The story ends where the shepherd promises were always headed. The worthless shepherd and his like are cast down, and the Lamb is the shepherd of the great multitude, Revelation 7:17, who 'will lead them to springs of living water.' The doomed flock is a flock redeemed, and the sale that marked it for slaughter is reversed by a purchase that marks it as God's own, Revelation 5:9. The final city has no shepherd who devours, and every tear is wiped away.

quiz.q: What do the two staffs, Favor and Union, represent?

options.text: God's gracious protection and the God-given unity of His people.
options.note: Favor is gracious protection, Union the bond of brotherhood, both broken at rejection.

options.text: The wealth and armies of the nations.
options.note: They represent God's grace and the people's unity, not worldly power.

options.text: Two literal weapons for battle.
options.note: They are symbolic shepherd's staffs, not weapons.

options.text: Nothing in particular.
options.note: They clearly symbolize grace and union, both cut in two.

quiz.q: What price was weighed out as the shepherd's wages?

options.text: Thirty pieces of silver, the price of a slave, an insulting valuation.
options.note: Thirty pieces of silver was the compensation for a slave in Exodus.

options.text: A generous fortune in gold.
options.note: The sum was a contemptibly low insult, not a fortune.

options.text: Nothing at all.
options.note: They did weigh out wages, thirty pieces of silver.

options.text: A share of the temple treasury.
options.note: It was thirty pieces of silver, later thrown to the potter.

quiz.q: How is this prophecy fulfilled in the New Testament?

options.text: Judas betrayed Jesus for thirty pieces of silver, later used to buy the potter's field.
options.note: Matthew 27 cites this prophecy for the silver and the potter's field.

options.text: Jesus paid thirty pieces of silver to His disciples.
options.note: The silver was the betrayal price paid to Judas, not paid by Jesus.

options.text: The Romans returned thirty coins to Israel.
options.note: The fulfillment is Judas's betrayal price and the potter's field.

options.text: It is never fulfilled.
options.note: Matthew explicitly ties it to Christ's betrayal.

quiz.q: What happens when the good shepherd is rejected?

options.text: Grace and union are broken, and a worthless, devouring shepherd is raised up.
options.note: The staffs are cut in two and a foolish shepherd takes his place.

options.text: The flock immediately prospers on its own.
options.note: The opposite: they are handed over to a devouring shepherd.

options.text: God abandons the world entirely.
options.note: God judges through bad leadership but still pronounces woe on the false shepherd.

options.text: Nothing changes at all.
options.note: Grace and union are broken and a worthless shepherd arises.

quiz.q: What is pronounced on the worthless shepherd?

options.text: Woe, with judgment on his arm and right eye for deserting the flock.
options.note: Verse 17 pronounces woe and judgment on the worthless shepherd.

options.text: Blessing and long life.
options.note: The opposite: woe and judgment, not blessing.

options.text: Promotion to king.
options.note: He is judged with woe, not exalted.

options.text: Nothing is said about him.
options.note: A clear woe and judgment are pronounced on him.

questions: The people valued the good Shepherd at a slave's price. In what subtle ways might you undervalue Christ and what He has done for you?
When the Shepherd was rejected, grace and unity were broken. Where do you see the loss of God's grace or of unity where His care has been spurned?
Christ came to His own and was not received. How does the cost of His rejection deepen your gratitude for His faithfulness to you?
God gave the people over to a devouring shepherd. How careful are you about whose leadership and voices you allow to shape your soul?
The whole betrayal was foretold in exact detail. How does God's sovereignty over even Christ's betrayal strengthen your trust in His larger plan?

translationNotes.note: The two staffs are named Favor, noam, and Union, chovlim; some render Union as Bonds. They picture God's gracious protection and the unity of His people, both later cut in two.
Thirty pieces of silver was the compensation set for a slave gored by an ox in Exodus 21:32, a contemptibly low valuation of the Shepherd, cited in Matthew 27:9.
Throw it to the potter renders a gesture of contemptuous disposal at the temple; Matthew 27:7-10 records the betrayal money buying the potter's field, tying the two together.
